speaker: tiffanyspeir
text: I'm just going to walk you quickly through a status update for what's happening with some regional planning efforts, starting with Vision 2050. The last time we went through some of this information, we didn't have Mr. Combs or Mr. Larson on the commission. So I'll just walk you through this quickly, but land use law in five minutes or less in Washington State. We start with the Growth Management Act, which is the foundation for what all of you do ultimately on the Planning Commission. It's the state statute that says there's urban areas, there's rural areas, and within the urban areas is where we're going to plan for our growth. And then it has a lot more detail obviously than that, but the cities are where most growth is anticipated to happen in state law. Then you have what are called multi-county planning policies and for us in the Central Puget Sound, that is called Vision 2050, meaning we're looking at it in 2020, and 2050 is the planning end horizon for this document. It's put together by what's called the Puget Sound Regional Council, and it covers King, Snohomish, Kitsap, and Pierce Counties. That's why it's called the multi-county planning policies. So those policies going back up the ladder have to be consistent with the GMA, but also the next level down, you have countywide planning policies. So in Pierce County, there are Pierce County countywide policies. They have to be consistent in turn with Vision 2050. In the bottom of this little rainbow, you see comprehensive plans. And so the City of Lakewood's comprehensive plan and its development regulations have to be consistent with the countywide planning policies, multi-county planning policies, and the Growth Management Act. So a lot of different layers here when you finally get down to writing city code or administering regulations. Vision 2050 was just updated, and it happens every 10 years. And so Vision 2040 was replaced by 2050 last October. And we're now in the process at the regional level of having PSRC start to roll out implementation guidance. So saying cities and counties, as you start looking at the countywide planning policies you deal with to how to update them, here's some suggestions. But then the other things that happen are allocations of population to various jurisdictions, including Lakewood, and that's called the Regional Growth Strategy. So these things are now starting to happen as after effects, if you will, of the adoption of Vision 2050. So basically Vision 2040 was in place for 10 years. It had a strategy for growth for the whole area. There were planning policies and actions related to them. In Vision 2050, it's the same thing. But some new tweaks on Vision 2050, there's a much more of a focus on regional effort. And for the first time, we're talking about housing as a regional process, a regional planning item. So rather than just the city of Lakewood planning for the housing it's supposed to have within its borders, for instance, it's now becoming a discussion about up and down the I-5 corridor, throughout Pierce County, how do we all work together to help ensure affordable housing for everyone? There's also new discussions about incorporating equity and health recognition, I guess I'll say, in all of the actions. So for instance, understanding that the way a city is laid out can affect people's public health, whether it's because they are living next to a transit or a traffic hub, or whether they're able to walk to where they work or walk to where they go to school, that affects people's public health. And then there's also within Vision 2050, a number of other things that fall out of it. So the transportation plan, economic strategy, regional centers framework, and others as well. All of this is gonna be incorporated into countywide planning policies by 2022. And then the city of Lakewood has until 2024 to update its individual comprehensive plan to be consistent with all of this new stuff. Speaking of the regional growth strategy, this is an effort and then ultimately a document that says all of the jurisdictions in Pierce County, but including Lakewood, this is the number of people you're supposed to be planning for. And within the growth strategy, there's different types of cities based on their size. And so here in Pierce County, Lakewood, Puyallup, and University Place are all called quote core cities. They are the big ones after Tacoma, which is called a metropolitan city. And the way the population was allocated, long story short, these three jurisdictions have been assigned quote 85,000 people by 2050 that they need to absorb and also 44,000 jobs. This process where the sausage is now made, where those three jurisdictions are negotiating with each other and potentially other cities that are called other types to help absorb these people, either the number itself or more or less, depending on what's happening in any individual jurisdiction. So within the city of Lakewood, there's also a regional growth strategy, I'm sorry, a regional growth center. It is the same as our downtown sub area. It's where most of the growth and most of the jobs are located and planned for within the city. So it's planned by 20 years after the adoption of that sub area. There's gonna be quite a few more people living there and quite a few more jobs. And that's consistent with Vision 2050. The other thing that's within the city is not only that regional growth center in the downtown, but a high capacity transit station, the Sounder Station. There's also the Pierce Transit Hub in the downtown. But the idea under Vision 2050 is growth is supposed to be encouraged near these high capacity transit stations and within regional growth centers. So what we have already is our downtown sub area, which is right there in the center. And then we're also, as you know, looking at the council adopting the Lakewood Station sub area which incorporates the Sounder Station here within the next month. Going back to that idea that Lakewood, Puyallup and University Place are supposed to be absorbing 85,000 additional people by 2050. The city of Lakewood took a look at those numbers. The response was actually transmitted back to Pierce County and the consultant working with them on assigning these individualized numbers to all of the cities in February. That basically said, given a number of different realities within the city of Lakewood, the number that you think we're going to absorb is not gonna happen. They had assigned the city 72,000 people by 2030 and an even higher number by 2050. However, there's a number of reasons why the city is saying that's not going to happen. And let me back up, I'm sorry. Between the 20 year period of 2000 to 2020, Lakewood has grown a total of 3%, meaning an average of 0.1% growth per year. And so the idea that it's suddenly going to grow by tens of thousands in the next 10 years or so is just completely out of range of what's happened historically. Secondly, and you know this already, but Lakewood is not a full service city, meaning the agencies that govern water, sewer, power and emergency services are all separate agencies from the city. And so the idea of trying to do long range planning and growth planning like other jurisdictions might do can't happen in Lakewood. There's a lot of coordination needed and there's also decisions that are made outside of the city's control regarding capacity. Third, within the city, there was a calculation done. There's a total of a little over 12,000 acres of the city. But because of certain land uses that again, the city is not going to see change, it can't in some cases change them. The development capacity within the city is reduced by a total of 52%, meaning more than half of the city's acreage is not available for additional densification over time. And what you see here is that list. There's the area on the east side of the city with air corridor zones and the clear zone near where McCord Field airplanes fly. There's the military lands themselves. Then there's a number of acres involved with Western State Hospital campus, Pierce and Clover Park Colleges, the hospital complex, St. Clair's I should say, Clover Park, Sound and Pierce Transit and then other city owned properties. That's 20% of the city there of itself. Another 14% are the lakes. And then there's 13% in addition to that of open space. So if you add all of that up, again, it's 52% of the city's acreage. And so here's a map of where within the city, the black areas are areas that are just not available for any additional growth. So this whole part over here, which is mostly residential, this needs to eventually get less dense, not more so in order to comply with Department of Defense and FAA guidance on safety in being so close to McCord. You've got the Western State Hospital complex and you've got some public institutional here, but there's other things throughout the city where there's just not the capacity to grow. So rather than the large number that which was 80,000 or something for the city by 2050, the city has requested 68,000 instead based on all of these things that I've just gone through. And then to go along with those ideas that you see in Vision 2050 about how you're supposed to be planning for growth near transit and taking advantage of those transit centers, the city has within the last two or three years adopted the downtown sub area plan and is about to adopt the Lakewood Station District one. And between those two, you're going to get up to 9,500 more people just within those two sub areas if all the planning is correct and we end up with that type of density and then a number of jobs as well. So we're in the middle of that discussion with Pierce County and the other core cities that will wrap up later this summer. The County Council will be adopting the new countywide planning policies consistent with that higher level with the Vision 2050 stuff by next spring. And then by 2024, as I mentioned earlier, Lakewood needs to have updated its comprehensive plan and development code to be consistent with Vision 2050 and the new countywide planning policies. And so I don't know if Mr. Buer wants to add any more to that, but just wanted to give you a progress update. And then what happens is this sausage-making process where the county then says, okay, we have 23 cities and the unincorporated area, and various cities are at different sizes right now. That's why we're called a core city. You as core cities are gonna take, I've just thrown a number, 10% of the total growth. So $7 million more or less should arrive. The Rescue Act is a lot different than the CARES Act last year. If you remember the CARES Act, all the money was supposed to be spent by the end of 2020, and it was very prescriptive. And cities like Lakewood did not get anything. In fact, the county got the money and the state got the money, and they were supposed to give it out to places like Lakewood, and we did get some. A lot of the other things like rent relief and those kinds of things are coming down in what I call other tranches. Through other means, there's business relief in there also. So, and this money can be spent over four years. We have until December 31st, 2024 to spend it. And we can also use it to replace lost revenue from last year. So there's a lot of things to consider that in the CARES Act, we didn't have to consider, or we didn't really have the choice to consider. So this is an interesting thing. It is a lot of money.
